title: Log cabin lap throw
subtitle: A 100 by 120 cm lap throw built from log-cabin garter rectangles in two colours.
excerpt: A 100 by 120 cm lap throw built by the log-cabin construction method: starting with a small centre square and adding garter-stitch strips in two alternating colours, rotating around the centre. The structure builds modularly; each strip is short and quick. About 400 g of each of two DK colours.
sourceNotes: Elizabeth Zimmermann, Knitting Without Tears (1971), §Log Cabin Squares, popularised the log-cabin blanket construction. The method is also described in Walker's A Treasury of Knitting Patterns (1968), §Log Cabin Stitch, as a standard modular garter structure.

glossaryTerms.definition: A modular knitting method where a small centre square is worked first, then successive strips of garter stitch are picked up along one edge at a time and worked outward. Each strip goes around the previous block, adding width and height in rotation. The finished piece has concentric square or rectangular rings of colour radiating from the centre.

content.text: A lap throw built by
log-cabin construction
on 4 mm needles using two DK colours, finishing at 100 cm wide by 120 cm long.

The log-cabin method is ideal for a project that must be set down and resumed frequently: each strip is short, independent, and complete in itself. Colour A and Colour B alternate: strips in Colour A run horizontally; strips in Colour B run vertically relative to the previous strip. The concentric-ring visual emerges automatically from the rotation. Budget about 400 g of each colour (about 880 m / 960 yards per colour) of DK. Individual strips use about 20 to 40 g each, so the project is also a good use of DK stash yarn.
What you need

items.name: Yarn A (main)
items.qty: 400 g (about 880 m / 960 yards) of DK in a solid or heathered colour

items.name: Yarn B (contrast)
items.qty: 400 g of DK in a contrasting colour

items.name: Needles
items.qty: 4 mm (UK 8 / US 6) needles, straight or circular 60 cm or longer

content.text: Gauge

22 stitches and 44 rows to 10 cm in garter stitch on 4 mm needles. At this gauge, a 5 cm centre square uses 11 stitches and 22 rows. Each subsequent strip adds approximately 1 cm to each dimension per 4-row pass (2 rows = 1 garter ridge = about 0.45 cm). The total strip count to reach 100 × 120 cm is approximately 56 strips.
At 20 stitches per 10 cm, the initial cast-on and all strip pick-up counts should be adjusted proportionally (multiply target cm by 2 rather than 2.2).
Stitches used

items.name: PU
items.qty: pick up stitches along an edge: 1 st per garter ridge (every 2 rows)

content.text: Pattern
Centre square

Using Colour A and the long-tail cast-on, cast on 11 stitches. Long-tail tail: (4 × 11) / 10 + 15 = 4.4 + 15 = 19.4 cm. Measure 25 cm. Knit every row (garter stitch) for 22 rows, producing a 5 cm × 5 cm square. Do not cast off.
Adding strips

After the centre square, rotate 90 degrees clockwise. With Colour B, pick up 11 stitches along the right edge of the centre square (1 per ridge), then work 8 rows of garter, this strip is 8 rows deep, adding approximately 2 cm. Turn 90 degrees clockwise again.

Each successive strip picks up stitches along the new edge (previous strip depth plus previous rectangle width) and works 8 garter rows. Colour alternates every strip rotation. Continue rotating clockwise and adding strips until the overall dimensions reach 100 cm wide by 120 cm long.
When you set this aside between sessions, note the current strip number, the current colour, and the current rotation direction.
Stitch count check-ins

After the first strip (Colour B, about 7 cm wide): count the stitches across the strip. Each new strip should have a stitch count equal to (centre width or previous-strip depth in stitches) plus any pick-up stitches from the adjacent edge. Recount at the midpoint (approximately 60 cm across) to confirm the rotation is producing the correct overall width.
Common faults

Pick-up count incorrect: too many or too few stitches were picked up along the previous edge. Pick up 1 stitch per garter ridge (every 2 rows) for a square pickup rate. An incorrect count causes the new strip to pucker or gap.
Rotation reversed: a strip was added in the wrong direction, producing an asymmetric block. After each strip, step back and confirm the colour ring is complete before picking up for the next strip.
Cast-off
Cast off each strip knitwise after its 8 rows before the next pick-up. Cast off the final border strips last.
Finishing
Weave in all ends. The garter fabric lies flat; no blocking is needed unless strips have varying tensions.
Care
Machine wash on a gentle 30-degree cycle for superwash DK. Lay flat to dry.
What to try next

From two-colour log cabin, try a three-colour log cabin: each complete rotation around the growing rectangle uses one of three colours in order. The concentric rings display all three colours in a repeating sequence.
